source.title: Influential Rank: A New Perspective of Post-training for Robust Model against Noisy Labels
source.authors: Seulki Park; Hwanjun Song; Daeho Um; D. Jo; Sangdoo Yun; Jin-Young Choi

page_placements.theme: Identifying corrupted supervision depends on the diagnostic and training conditions

record.file_problem: none; full paper and supplementary material supplied
record.tranche_reason: The paper relies on the premise that deep networks overfit noisy labels, then uses influence scores to detect and remove suspected mislabeled samples. Its results evaluate that post-training method, not whether the claim versions hold.
record.gate_note: The paper reports noisy-label detection precision and influence-score behavior. It does not report fitting random labels, training error at the tested noise rates, or learning real labels before noisy labels. The reported test accuracies for robust post-training methods do not measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study uses noisy-label overfitting to develop and evaluate Influential Rank. Detection precision, influence scores and post-training test accuracy do not establish any claim version. Figure 4 reports near-zero training losses for DivideMix at 40% symmetric noise, but does not establish perfect fitting across corruption rates or compare learning order.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that Influential Rank improves multiple pretrained robust-learning methods and can also detect mislabeled videos or regularize models trained on clean data.
record.recipe_differences: The study starts from models trained on noisy-label datasets and applies post-training that scores, removes, and relabels influential samples. It does not reproduce the random-label memorization experiments in the cited original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise rate and dataset type are varied; the reported noise-detection precision differs across those conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Influential Rank detects mislabeled examples with condition-dependent precision after two post-training rounds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Influence-based post-training can identify mislabeled examples in synthetic and human-annotated noisy image datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 4.3.1 and Figure 4 describe near-zero training losses for clean and noisy examples after DivideMix training at 40% symmetric noise; the toy experiment illustrates a boundary distorted around mislabeled points.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Trained networks can exhibit low losses on noisy examples and distorted decision boundaries under partial label corruption.

record.code_released: https://github.com/yjxiong/tsn-pytorch (the paper says code will be made publicly available after publication; this URL is for TSN code)
record.problems: The supplied results do not report training error for the noisy-label experiments. Detection-precision results are averaged across three noise realizations, but no uncertainty interval is given. The CIFAR-10N table is flattened, and the CE value for the Worst condition cannot be assigned from the supplied layout.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports many additional detection-precision entries in Supplementary Material Table 10 for other methods and datasets; they were omitted to keep the extracted sample concise. It also reports test-accuracy comparisons in Tables 1, 3, 4, 5, 11, and 12, but these evaluate the proposed post-training method and do not measure a claim version.

untested.parts: Completely random labels, zero or near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Time to fit true versus random labels and convergence speed as corruption increases. Additional post-training epochs do not measure this.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training fit across corruption fractions and the joint progression of training fit and test error from clean to completely random labels. Baseline test accuracies decline at 20%, 50% and 70% noise, but training fit is not reported across those conditions.
Whether weight decay, dropout or augmentation prevent random-label fitting, and whether removing them preserves true-label generalization.
Learning shared real-label patterns before memorizing noise. The paper cites this premise but provides no temporal comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The displaced Worst column in Table 10(b) is recoverable from its six entries and the six method rows. Near-zero loss and qualitative boundary distortion do not supply the missing complete-randomization, corruption-sweep training-fit or learning-order measurements.

versions.untested_parts: No completely random labeling experiment, chance-level test error result, or comparison holding architecture and training hyperparameters fixed.
No comparison of time to fit true versus random labels or convergence speed across corruption fractions.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiment.
Although synthetic label-noise rates are varied, the paper does not report training error across those rates or test whether networks fit all examples perfectly while test error rises steadily.
No experiment testing whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation prevent fitting random labels or affect generalization after their removal.
No analysis of learning order comparing real-label patterns with noisy or random labels over training.

relation.reason: Noisy-label overfitting motivates and enables Influential Rank; the reported experiments evaluate the method rather than test the catalog's claim versions.

tranche.reason: The study exploits noisy-label overfitting to develop and evaluate post-training detection and mitigation. Its detection precision and test accuracy do not establish any claim version. Figure 4 describes normalized training losses close to zero at 40% symmetric noise, without establishing perfect training fit or the claimed training dynamics.

source_check.notes: R1–R3 are method-performance results, not evidence of random-label fitting; their versions=none and cannot_determine states are appropriate. The supplied text is arXiv v4 dated 19 April 2023, although the record lists 2021.
